analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to protect workers from extreme heat with water, shade, paid rest breaks, and safety plans.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after introduction, it was referred to the Senate labor committee, which took no action before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Labor Department to write a nationwide workplace heat standard requiring employers to provide cool drinking water, paid rest breaks, shade or cool-down areas, acclimatization schedules for new workers, training, and emergency response plans. It is named for Asunción Valdivia, a farmworker who died of heat stroke after picking grapes in 105-degree California heat. It also would have given the Labor Department one year to issue an interim final rule, extended the time limit for heat-safety citations to four years, and added whistleblower protections for workers who report heat hazards.
analysis.who_benefits: Outdoor and hot-indoor workers — farmworkers, construction crews, warehouse and delivery workers, restaurant and kitchen staff — who face heat stress on the job. Many are immigrants or low-wage workers. The bill would require employers to pay for protective equipment, hydration, and the rest breaks and training time, so workers would not lose pay for safety measures. It also would have required all safety materials in a language workers understand.

how_it_helps.text: Each employer would have had to furnish a workplace free from conditions that could reasonably cause death or serious harm from heat stress, with the Labor Department writing the enforceable standard [S2].

The core required program includes cool potable water at employer expense, periodic paid rest breaks to reduce heat stress, access to shade or cool-down spaces, and acclimatization policies for workers adjusting to heat [S2].

Required training, posters, and written plans would have to be provided in English and a language the employees understand, tailored to workers' literacy — aimed at groups like Spanish-speaking farmworkers [S2].

Workers would get whistleblower protection: an employee punished for raising heat-safety concerns could file a complaint and, if the Labor Department declines to act, sue in federal court for relief plus attorney's fees [S2].

The bill extended the deadline for issuing a citation for a heat-safety violation from the standard six months to four years after the violation, and required paid regular-rate compensation for mandated rest breaks, training, and medical removal protection [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers in heat-exposed industries — agriculture, construction, warehousing and delivery, landscaping, and kitchens — would bear the cost of water, shade or cooling, paid break time, training, engineering controls such as ventilation or climate control, and written prevention plans.

drawbacks.text: The Labor Department would have had to issue an interim final rule within one year without following the normal multi-year rulemaking process, including skipping paperwork-reduction review — a speed critics would call rushed for a standard covering most of the economy [S2].

The bill instructs the Secretary to place 'preeminent value' on worker protection in weighing rulemaking considerations and presumes state heat rules are feasible, which would tilt the standard toward the most protective, most costly requirements employers would have to fund [S2].

Small employers — family farms, small contractors — would face the same water, shade, break, and recordkeeping obligations as large firms, and compliance costs could be proportionally heavier for them.

The bill directs standards to attain 'the highest degree of health and safety protection to the extent feasible,' and courts defer heavily to the Secretary's interpretation — language that would have limited employers' ability to challenge requirements they consider impractical [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Heat kills and sickens workers, and farmworkers, construction crews, and warehouse staff have among the highest exposure. The costs fall on employers, and many provisions — water, shade, breaks — are cheap relative to the risk, which is why several states including California already impose similar rules that the bill itself cites as proof of feasibility. The bill's one-year shortcut around normal rulemaking and its deference-heavy design are the fair criticisms: it trades process for speed, which raises the odds of overbroad requirements but also reflects that no federal heat standard existed despite years of heat-related deaths.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never acted on it, and the bill died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Sherrod Brown introduced the bill on July 26, 2023, with 18 original cosponsors [S1][S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the day it was introduced [S4].
The committee took no further action — no markup, no hearing on the bill, no vote — and the full Senate never considered it [S4].
It ended the 118th Congress with 25 cosponsors, all Democrats or independents, and no Republican support [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Heat-exposed employers avoided the cost of mandatory water, shade, paid breaks, and heat plans, while workers exposed to dangerous heat continue without any federal heat-safety standard.

for.name: Sherrod Brown
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it in the Senate.

for.name: 24 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; half the Democratic caucus signed on, alongside 1 of 4 independents.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and took no action on it — no markup, hearing, or vote — for the remaining 17 months of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 25 cosponsors were Democrats or independents — 24 of 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 4 independents — with no Republican support, and the bill never advanced past committee.

industries.note: Farm work carries some of the highest heat-death risk, and the bill would have required water, shade, paid breaks, acclimatization plans, and revised standards for temporary labor camps, all at employer expense. Farmworkers, many Spanish-speaking, would be the direct beneficiaries.

Crews working in summer heat would have gained mandated hydration, rest breaks, and heat plans; contractors would absorb the cost of break time and compliance. The bill would also have allowed engineering controls like ventilation or climate control.
Hot warehouses and delivery routes fall under the heat-stress definition, so large logistics employers would have faced written prevention plans, training, and paid cool-down time.
Commercial kitchens are a defined heat source, and kitchen staff would have gained protection standards; restaurant operators would bear the cost.
